title: Philemon 1:1–7
context: Paul writes as a prisoner to Philemon and the church meeting in his house. Thanksgiving for Philemon’s faith and refreshing love prepares an appeal concerning Onesimus. The opening makes a personal matter part of the community’s shared life in Christ. Arminian and Reformed readers largely agree that received grace should become practical fellowship.

verses.text: Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, to Philemon, our beloved fellow worker,
verses.arminianNotes: Paul introduces himself through imprisonment for Christ and calls Philemon a beloved coworker. Arminian readers see a relationship of shared service rather than mere rank. The appeal that follows will ask love to shape conduct within this fellowship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that Paul begins with fellowship and costly service rather than an assertion of apostolic office. Philemon is addressed as a partner in Christ’s work. This relational opening prepares a request grounded in their common belonging to Jesus.

verses.text: to the beloved Apphia, to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the assembly in your house:
verses.arminianNotes: The greeting extends beyond Philemon to named believers and the church in his house. Arminian readers see that personal reconciliation has communal significance. The letter does not identify Apphia’s and Archippus’s precise family relationships, so those should not be assumed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the household gathering as a community that shares responsibility for living out the gospel. The request to Philemon is personal but not isolated from the church. Naming fellow believers places the appeal within accountable Christian fellowship.

verses.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verses.arminianNotes: Grace and peace come from the Father and Jesus Christ before Paul asks anything of Philemon. Arminian readers see divine generosity as the source of loving action. Reconciliation is a response to grace, not a way to purchase God’s favor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the blessing grounding the letter’s ethical appeal in God’s gift. Peace with God should bear fruit in peace among believers. Both traditions understand Christian obedience as flowing from grace rather than creating it.

verses.text: I thank my God always, making mention of you in my prayers,
verses.arminianNotes: Paul thanks God for Philemon and remembers him in prayer. Arminian readers see gratitude for grace at work in another person, alongside continuing dependence on God. Prayer accompanies the appeal rather than functioning as a substitute for practical engagement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Paul gives God credit for the good he sees in Philemon. Thanksgiving and petition belong together because grace both begins and sustains Christian life. The coming request rests on prayerful fellowship, not mere pressure.

verses.text: hearing of your love and of the faith which you have toward the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints,
verses.arminianNotes: Philemon’s faith in the Lord and love for the saints are already known to Paul. Arminian readers see living trust expressing itself in care for others. Paul appeals to an established pattern of love rather than inventing an entirely new obligation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see love for believers as the fruit of faith in Christ. Paul’s praise does not make love the ground of acceptance with God. It identifies the gospel’s visible effect, which the appeal concerning Onesimus will bring into sharper focus.

verses.text: that the fellowship of your faith may become effective in the knowledge of every good thing which is in us in Christ Jesus.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul prays that shared faith will become effective through fuller recognition of the good found in Christ. Arminian readers see fellowship maturing through active participation. Faith is not merely private conviction; it opens believers to the gifts and needs of others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see fellowship in Christ producing practical fruit as believers recognize their shared blessings. The prayer anticipates Paul’s later appeal to receive Onesimus as a partner. Understanding the good given in Christ should deepen generous participation in his people’s life.

verses.text: For we have much joy and comfort in your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother.
verses.arminianNotes: Philemon’s love has brought real refreshment to the saints. Arminian readers see encouragement that grace-enabled choices can strengthen an entire community. The appeal will ask him to extend this same refreshing care to a person whose reception may be difficult.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see existing love as evidence of God’s work in Philemon and a fitting basis for confidence. Paul will later ask that his own heart be refreshed. The thanksgiving gently connects past kindness with the reconciliation now being requested.
